name: Jagalchi Market
label: Jagalchi Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '자갈치시장' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '자갈치시장' (way/502017125): edge nearest the subject (902 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/382696296: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jalgachi Fish Market' (159 m across).
notes: Korea's largest seafood market by the harbour.

text.description:
Jagalchi Market is generally considered the largest fish market in South Korea, and it sits right on the edge of Nampo Port. It is one of the ten landmarks of Busan. The name is said to come from jagal, the Korean word for gravel, because the market was once surrounded by gravel. The market is also known for its female vendors, the "Jagalchi Ajumma", a name that goes back to the years after the Korean War, when women sold goods on the streets here.

For a phone photo, skip the crowded aisles for a moment and walk out to the seaside area behind the market building, along Jagalchi Coast Road. From here you see the seaward side of the building with the harbour, ships and open water behind it. It is a calmer, wider picture than anything you will get among the stalls, and it shows the market in its real setting beside the water.

Keep the building and a strip of water in the same frame so the picture explains itself. Ships and boats make good foreground or background interest, so wait for a gap in passers-by before you shoot. If you want more variety, BIFF Square and the Yeongdo Bridge area are worth a look as well. The market also hosts the Busan Jagalchi Festival in autumn, which may add colour if you are visiting then.
text.geographic_location: Jagalchi Market is in Busan on the edge of Nampo Port, close to the Yeongdo Grand Bridge. The seaside walk behind the market building runs along Jagalchi Coast Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Jagalchi Market (자갈치시장) at Nampo Port in Busan, for example by taxi or with a map app. For the seaward view described here, walk round to the water side of the market building, along Jagalchi Coast Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the market building with the water behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole length of the building and a big sweep of harbour. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single ship or a detail on the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (seaside area behind the market building, along Jagalchi Coast Road). The market building's seaward side with the harbor, ships and open water in the background. From that point the building sits between you and the water, so for the seaward view, walk round to the seaside area behind the market building, along Jagalchi Coast Road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the building's seaward side on one third of the frame, with the water and ships filling the rest. Keep the horizon level. If you prefer a different view, BIFF Square gives a picture of the street markers and people moving past the market area. The Yeongdo Bridge gives a wider harbour panorama, but frame it carefully because the market may be small or hard to see from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky and water do not wash out. Take a Live Photo if boats are moving, so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the market is busy and the harbour is easy to see. Softer light in the morning or late afternoon usually flatters the water.

text.access_note: The seaside area behind the market is a free public space, but opening and closing days for the market itself vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Softer morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters harbour scenes.
The market is busiest in daytime, and passers-by can get into the frame on the seaside walk.

name: Haeundae Beach
label: Haeundae Beach
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/107531972: large area 'Haeundae Beach' (1477 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Busan's most famous beach with the high-rise skyline behind.

text.description: Haeundae Beach is a long, wide city beach in Busan, with a skyline of tall high-rise towers behind the sand. That mix of open sand, sea and high-rises is why it photographs well. The sandy stretch is about 1.46 kilometres long and 40 metres wide, so you can step back, find a clear view and fit a lot into the frame. The beach is open all year and holds events through the seasons, including a Polar Bear Festival each January and a sand festival, so you may find sand sculptures, stages or crowds in your shot. It first opened in 1965 and was the largest beach in the country at the time. Before that it was a fishing area, and it has been a leisure space since the late 19th century. In 2008 it set a Guinness World Record for the most beach umbrellas, 7,937, so a busy summer day really is busy. For a phone photo, keep the horizon level and include something in the foreground, such as footprints in the sand, a line of umbrellas or the edge of a wave. Tall buildings such as the LCT Towers are visible from the beach and make a strong backdrop. Wipe your lens, as sea spray and sand dust are common on beaches.
text.geographic_location: Haeundae Beach is in Haeundae District, Busan. Dongbaekseom, a former island, is at its west end.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so use the map to reach the Haeundae District seafront. Follow the map and keep the sea on your side as you walk along the beach. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of sand, sea and towers. Switch to the default lens (1x) for people and umbrellas without stretching the edges. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the high-rises or a single detail on the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line so it stays level. Put footprints, a row of umbrellas or the water's edge in the foreground so the eye is led into the picture. Keep the towers on one side rather than cutting through the middle. For a very wide scene, try panorama mode and move slowly and steadily.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand or the people to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the bright sky is washing out the picture. Turn on Live Photos if waves are breaking, so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. In the evening, night mode can pick up the lit-up towers, but rest your phone on something steady or brace your elbows.

text.access_note: The beach is an open public space that stays open all year, though events can change what is on the sand, so check the official site before you go if you plan to visit during a festival.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and fewer people on the beach.
Sea spray and sand dust can get onto a phone lens at a beach.
At night the towers behind the beach are lit up, so night mode can work well there.

name: Gamcheon Culture Village
label: Gamcheon Village
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Little Prince viewpoint' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'New Little Prince Statue' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/382693934: large area 'Gamcheon Culture Village' (803 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Hillside village of pastel houses and murals.

text.description:
Gamcheon Culture Village is a hillside neighbourhood in Busan, made up of steep, winding lanes and brightly painted houses stacked up the slope. It was built in the 1920s and 1930s, and a public art project that began in 2009 turned it into the colourful, artistic place visitors see today. Art students, artists and residents added sculptures, murals and small installations, including scenes from the Little Prince. It is sometimes nicknamed "Korea's Santorini".

It photographs well because the houses climb the hill in layers, so you get rows of colourful rooftops with the sea beyond. The best-known frame is at the Little Prince viewpoint, a terrace with the Little Prince and Fox statue. It sits roughly midway along the main walking route. Here you can put the statue in the foreground and the pastel rooftops behind it, or photograph a friend sitting beside it. Expect a queue at busy times, especially midday and weekends, so early morning is easier.

If you want a different view, Haneul Maru gives the classic panorama of rooftops with the port beyond. Allow plenty of time, because the lanes are steep and you will want to stop often. Check the official site before you go for current access details.
text.geographic_location: Gamcheon Culture Village is in Gamcheon-dong, in Busan's Saha District, spread across a steep hillside slope above the port.
text.directions_text: The village is in Gamcheon-dong, Saha District, Busan. From there the heart of the village is to the south, about 3 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue and a person beside it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the layered rooftops. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), try 2x to pick out a single group of colourful houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Little Prince viewpoint (the terrace with the Little Prince and Fox statue, roughly midway along the main walking route). The Little Prince and Fox statue in the foreground, looking out over the pastel rooftops toward the sea; a good photo of a person beside the statue. If the queue is long, Haneul Maru is a good alternative for a rooftop panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one side, leaving the rooftops and sea in the rest of the frame. For a portrait, keep your friend close to the statue so both are sharp. Try portrait mode if you want the background softened, but check the rooftops still look clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue or your friend to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few shots, as people often move in and out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, or the hour before sunset, will give you a shorter queue at the statue. Check the village's current opening times before planning a late visit, as shops and cafes reportedly close around six and some inner lanes are partly unlit after dark.

text.access_note: The village is an open neighbourhood where people live, but check the official site before you go for current access details.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit more of a wide rooftop view into one frame.
Portrait mode can soften the background behind a person standing next to the statue.
Lowering the exposure slider can stop a bright sky from washing out the picture.
The lanes are steep enough that walking between viewpoints takes longer than the distance suggests.

name: Haedong Yonggungsa
label: Haedong Yonggungsa
camera_source: Commons cluster (8 photos), weak. Moved 40 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 65 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/382701819: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Haedong Yonggungsa' (170 m across).
notes: Seaside temple on the cliffs of Gijang.

text.description: Haedong Yonggungsa is a Buddhist temple on the coast of Gijang-gun, in the east of Busan. It is one of few temples in Korea set on the seaside, and that is what makes it a good subject for a phone. Roofs, stone steps, lanterns and open water all fit into the same view. The temple says it was first built in 1376, though that date is disputed. It honours Haesu Gwaneum Daebul, the Sea Goddess Buddha of Mercy. The complex is large, and it is popular with visitors, particularly around Buddha's Birthday, when it is decorated with paper lanterns. For a phone, the simplest approach is to start wide and take in the whole setting: temple roofs with the sea behind. Then move closer for details such as lanterns, carved stonework and rooflines against the water. Turn on the gridlines so the horizon stays level, since the sea makes any tilt obvious. Walk slowly and look back as well as forward, because the angle changes a lot as you move through the grounds. Expect other visitors in the frame; wait a few seconds for a gap, or use them to show the scale of the place. Take a few shots of each view rather than one, as people and waves keep changing the picture.
text.geographic_location: On the coast of Gijang-gun, close to Haeundae Beach, on the east side of Busan. The temple sits right beside the sea.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check local transport options for getting to Haedong Yonggungsa from the Haeundae Beach area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the temple and the sea into one frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out lanterns, roof details and carvings without leaving your spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Yongmun-gyo (the bridge leading to the main hall, shooting back toward the halls). The golden-roofed halls stacked on the rocks with the sea behind them, the classic wide composition of the temple.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on a top or bottom line, so the sea does not tilt. Keep the temple roofs on one side and leave the other for open water, which gives the picture a clear shape. Use the ultra-wide for the full scene, then 2x or more for lanterns and rooflines. If people walk through, wait a moment or let them add scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple roofs to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or sea is bright, so the detail in the roofs is not washed out. If the sea is moving, try a Live Photo and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer and less crowded. Around Buddha's Birthday the paper lanterns make it more colourful, but it will be busier.

text.access_note: This is a working Buddhist temple, so dress modestly and be respectful; check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and any entry rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter than the rest of the day.
As a place of worship, modest dress and quiet behaviour are expected.
The stand-here point is on the northern side of the complex and faces south towards the main buildings.
The temple has entry arrangements that may change, so visitors should check them.

name: Gwangalli Beach
label: Gwangalli Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gwangalli Beach' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Gwangalli Beach'.
notes: Beach facing the illuminated Gwangan Bridge.

text.description:
Gwangalli Beach is a curved, half-moon stretch of fine sand in Suyeong District, tucked inside a cove that the Gwangan Bridge spans. It is about 1.4 km long and between 25 and 110 metres wide, so there is plenty of room to walk along the shore and try different angles. Behind the sand, alleys of restaurants and coffee shops give the promenade a lively look. The beach is also remembered as a location for the car chase in the 2018 film Black Panther.

It photographs well because the bridge sits directly ahead across the water. The middle of the beach is the classic postcard position. Stand on the sand just above the waterline and the whole span of the bridge fills the far side of the bay, with the beach and promenade framing the bottom of the picture. For the richest colour, try blue hour, about 20 to 30 minutes after sunset, when the bridge lights are on.

If you want the bridge bigger in the frame, Millak Waterside Park gets you much closer, with the Marine City towers behind. On Saturdays a free drone show is held over the bay and draws large crowds, so arrive well before it starts. Keep to the pedestrian areas and stay off the bridge access roads.
text.geographic_location: Gwangalli Beach is in Gwangan 2-dong, Suyeong District, Busan, just west of Haeundae Beach. It lies inside the cove crossed by the Gwangan Bridge.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app on your phone to navigate to Gwangalli Beach in Suyeong District. Walk onto the middle section of the sand to reach the phone icon on the map. Gwangalli Beach itself is about 5 minutes on foot to the north-east of it. The phone icon on the map is about 290 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the bridge across the bay with the beach below. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sand and promenade in the foreground, but the bridge will look smaller. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the bridge and its lights closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Stand on Gwangalli Beach, in the central section on the sand just above the waterline. The beach and promenade frame the lower edge of the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line so the bridge sits across the middle of the picture. Keep the phone level so the bridge does not slope. Let a strip of sand or the waterline run along the bottom for depth. For a closer, bigger bridge, Millak Waterside Park is a good alternative viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: At dusk, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone still. Tap on the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not wash out. A Live Photo can catch moving waves, but it is optional.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, about 20 to 30 minutes after sunset, when the bridge lights are on.

text.access_note: The beach is an open public space, but check the official site before you go for any event, such as the Saturday drone show, that may affect access.

name: Dongbaek Island
label: Dongbaek Island
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '황옥공주 인어상' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: '동백공원' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7866912597: the OpenStreetMap point 'Dongbaek Island'.
notes: Coastal walking path next to Haeundae.

text.description:
Dongbaekseom is a headland at the western end of Haeundae Beach. It used to be a true island, but soil gradually built up between it and the shore, and it is now part of the mainland. The name comes from camellia flowers, which are said to bloom here in large numbers. Busan made it a designated monument in 1999, and the poet Ch'oe Ch'i-wŏn is recorded as having visited. A walking trail circles the headland, with statues and carved inscriptions along the way, including the legendary Princess Hwangok mermaid statue and the Nurimaru APEC House.

The mermaid statue is a good place to start taking photos. It sits on the rocks by the shoreline with open sea behind it, so you can shoot it as a dark shape against the bright water. It is a calmer, more romantic picture than the wide views from the lighthouse. Keep your phone steady, leave plenty of sea in the frame, and take a few versions with the statue in different parts of the picture. If you have time, the lighthouse and the APEC House terrace give you wider views of the bay and Gwangan Bridge. The area is military-protected, so some coastal views are restricted. Follow the signs and stay on the path.
text.geographic_location: Dongbaekseom is in U-dong, Busan, at the western end of Haeundae Beach. It is a headland that was once an island.
text.directions_text: Start from the western end of Haeundae Beach, where the headland begins. Walk in from the western end of Haeundae Beach; motorbikes and bicycles cannot go onto the island. From the main path, follow the shoreline trail to the mermaid statue, which sits on the rocks below the coastal path. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the statue and a good amount of sea both fit in the frame. If you can't get close enough to the rocks, try telephoto (2x) to fill the frame with the statue. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (on the rocks by the shoreline, below the coastal path). The Princess Hwangok mermaid statue seated on the rocks with the sea behind it, which works well as a silhouette against the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the lines, with the open sea filling the rest of the frame. Crouch slightly so the statue stands out against the water rather than the land. If you have time, the Dongbaekseom Lighthouse, with Haeundae's curve and Gwangan Bridge behind it, makes a good second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: For a silhouette, tap on the bright sea to set focus, then slide the exposure down until the statue turns dark and the water keeps its colour. Take a normal shot too. Portrait mode is not needed here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is soft, is the time one guide recommends for this statue. The lighthouse view is best at golden hour.

text.access_note: This is an open coastal trail, but it is a military-protected area where some views are restricted, so follow the signs and confirm opening hours at the lighthouse and APEC House before you go.

pin_flags: area name label only (place=island): check the pin

name: Huinnyeoul Culture Village
label: Huinnyeoul Village
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '이송도전망대' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '이송도전망대' (way/1143190695): middle (20 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N6324143185 (Huinnyeoul Culture Village): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Cliffside village along the coast of Yeongdo.

text.description:
Huinnyeoul Culture Village is a seaside village of narrow lanes and steep steps, and it works well for phone photos because the sea keeps appearing between the buildings and the greenery. The picture most visitors come for is taken from the terrace called 이송도전망대 (Isongdo Observatory, also called the Huinnyeoul Observatory). It sits next to the piano stairs, on the village path. From there you look out over the open sea, framed by greenery, with the stairway running down below you. Guides treat it as the village's main photo spot.

To find it, walk the alley just before the piano stairs. If you have time, two other spots are worth a look. Inside the 흰여울해안터널 (coastal tunnel), you can take a silhouette or a portrait against the bright sea, and Namhang Bridge is sometimes visible in the opening. The 무지개계단 (rainbow stairs) give you colourful steps against the sky, or a sea view from the stairs themselves.

The tunnel and rainbow stairs are often crowded, so be patient and wait for a gap, or shoot a little wider and accept people as part of the scene. The lower coastal route involves climbing stairs, so wear comfortable shoes. Conditions can change, so check on the day.
text.geographic_location: Huinnyeoul Culture Village is on the Busan coast, a village of stepped lanes running down towards the sea. The viewpoint terrace is beside the piano stairs on the village path.
text.directions_text: No Metro station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Huinnyeoul Culture Village itself. Once in the village, follow the village path and take the alley just before the piano stairs to reach the terrace. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sea, the greenery and the stairway together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the terrace is busy or you want more of the stairs in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter view of the sea and the steps below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 이송도전망대 (next to the piano stairs, on the village path). The open sea framed by greenery and the stairway below, the classic village postcard view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Let the greenery frame the sides and the stairway lead the eye down to the sea. For something different, the tunnel is good for a silhouette or portrait against the bright opening, and the rainbow stairs work with the sky behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sea keeps its colour. In the tunnel, tap on the bright opening for a silhouette, or on your subject's face for a portrait.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light than midday, and the tunnel and rainbow stairs tend to be quieter at less busy times of day.

text.access_note: The village and its viewpoints are open public space and free to enter, but check current conditions before you go.

name: Oryukdo
label: Oryukdo Skywalk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '오륙도 스카이워크' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '오륙도 스카이워크' (node/4197185189): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/6995498: large area 'Oryukdo Islets' (902 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Rocky islets seen from a glass skywalk.

text.description:
Oryukdo is a small group of rocky islets just off the coast of Yongho-dong, in Busan's Nam District. The name means 'Five-Six Islands' because the count changes with the tide: the island nearest the shore can look like one or two. Only the outermost island, Deungdaeseom, is built on, and it carries a lighthouse. The rocks come from volcanic activity about 80 million years ago, worn down over time into the shapes you see now. The islets are protected and the public cannot visit them, so you photograph them from the shore.

The best-known place to do that is the Oryukdo Skywalk (오륙도 스카이워크), a U-shaped glass walkway that opened in 2013 on the cliff facing the islands. It works well for phone photos because the islets sit straight ahead and the sea opens out on both sides, so you get a clean, simple composition. The glass floor also lets you shoot down at the waves for a second kind of picture.

Take one wide shot of the whole scene, then a closer one of the islets. Wipe your lens before you start, as sea air leaves a film. Hold your phone firmly when you point it down through the glass. Weather matters here, because the glass floor closes in rain or strong wind.
text.geographic_location: Oryukdo lies off the coast at Yongho-dong in Busan's Nam District, in Busan Bay. The Skywalk is on the cliff facing the islets.
text.directions_text: Start from Yongho-dong in the Nam District and search for 오륙도 스카이워크 in a map app to find the route to the Oryukdo Skywalk. The islets lie to the south of the walkway, so once you are on it, look straight out to sea. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the U-shaped walkway and the sea on both sides. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the islets straight ahead. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the islets closer and pick out the lighthouse island.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (middle of the U-shaped glass walkway, looking out at the islets). Sea on both sides with the Oryukdo islets straight ahead, and downward views through the glass floor to the waves. Guides name the centre of the U as the best single photo position.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line, with the islets sitting just off-centre. Keep a little of the walkway rail or the glass edge in the corner of the wide shot to give a sense of scale. For a second picture, point the phone straight down through the glass at the waves. If you have time, the nearby 오륙도 해맞이공원 gives a wider view of the whole Skywalk together with the islets and sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the islets to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and sea keep their colour. Wipe the lens first. Live Photos can catch moving waves, and a short panorama along the sea works well from the middle of the walkway.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide suggests weekday mornings around 10-11am, when the light is less backlit.

text.access_note: The Skywalk is free to enter, shoe covers are required, the glass floor closes in rain or strong wind, and last admission is about 17:50 (Oct-May) or 18:50 (Jun-Sep), but check the official site before you go.

name: Gukje Market
label: Gukje Market
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/500548799: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gukje Market' (397 m across).

text.description:
Gukje Market is one of Busan's oldest working markets, set among the shops and lanes of Sinchang-dong in the Jung District. It began in 1945 as Dottaegi Market, a name that roughly means 'bustling market', and took its present name in 1950. During the Korean War, refugees arriving in Busan set up stalls here, and the market grew into a busy centre of trade. It was badly damaged by fire in 1953 and never quite regained its former size. Today it spreads across six zones and twelve buildings, selling tools, kitchenware, clothing and much more, with newer shops and eateries mixed in. Many visitors know the name from the 2014 film Ode to My Father, which takes its Korean title from the market.

For photographs, the appeal is everyday life: stacked goods, hanging signs, narrow passages and people going about their shopping. The market covers an area roughly 400 m across, so there is no single view. Walk in and look for repeating patterns, colourful displays and long perspectives down a lane. Keep your phone ready but be considerate: ask before taking close-up photos of stallholders or customers, and step aside from busy walkways when you stop to frame a shot.
text.geographic_location: Gukje Market is in Sinchang-dong, in Busan's Jung District, in the Nampodong area. It sits close to Jagalchi Market and Bupyeong Market.
text.directions_text: Head for the Nampodong area of the Jung District, which is the easiest place to start; the market can also be reached from Jagalchi and Nampo subway stations. If you are coming from further away, use the Jagalchi or Nampo subway stations and walk in. The phone icon on the map is about 340 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for narrow lanes and long views between stalls, and the default lens (1x) for most stall and street scenes. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as signs, goods and rooflines from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 340 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. Once inside, stand at a lane junction where you can see two or three directions at once.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up a lane so it runs toward the centre of the frame, with stalls on both sides. Include a person walking or a bright sign to give scale. Take a wider shot first, then a closer one of a single display or hanging sign. Portrait mode works well on neatly arranged goods.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a lane to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the highlights down slightly so signs do not burn out. Wipe the lens before you start, as market air can be dusty or greasy.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A weekday morning is usually calmer for open lanes, while late afternoon into evening brings lit signs; use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The market is a working shopping area; individual shops and buildings may keep their own hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The market lanes are narrow and busy, especially at midday and at weekends.
Weekday mornings are usually calmer than weekends.
Signs are lit in the evening, and night mode helps with low light.
It is polite to ask before taking close-up photos of stallholders or customers.
Shops and buildings in the market may keep their own opening hours.

name: Busan Tower
label: Busan Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/480601129: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Diamond Tower' (21 m across).
notes: Tower in Yongdusan Park with city and harbour views.

text.description:
Busan Tower is a 120-metre tower standing in Yongdusan Park, in Jung District. It was built in 1973 and is used purely for sightseeing: it has no transmitting equipment. At the top there is a deck with panoramic views and a small cafe, reached by two high-speed elevators during working hours. The base is linked to a few galleries and souvenir shops. Tourist guides often recommend it as a good place to look over the city's port.

For photographs, the tower works in two ways. From the ground it is a tall, slim shape that stands out against the sky, so it suits a vertical frame. If you go up, you can photograph the harbour and the city from above. Because the tower is so tall, the phone icon on the map sits right at its foot, so you will need to step back a little within the park to fit the whole thing in. Look for a clear gap in the trees and people before you shoot. Keep the phone upright, use the gridlines to keep the tower's sides straight, and take a few frames from slightly different distances. If you go up to the deck, hold the phone close to the glass, if there is any, to cut down on reflections.
text.geographic_location: Busan Tower is in Yongdusan Park, in Jung District, Busan.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Yongdusan Park in Jung District and head for the tower, which is tall enough to see from around the park. The phone icon on the map is at the foot of the tower, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the base to get the whole tower in, looking up. Use the default lens (1x) from a few steps back for a more natural shape. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the top of the tower and the deck.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Then walk a short way back along the park paths until the whole tower fits in your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright and turn on the gridlines. Line the tower up with a vertical grid line so its sides look straight, and leave a little sky above the top. Include some trees or the park's paths at the bottom to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright and the tower looks dark. If you are going up to the deck, tap on the view rather than the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives you a clear view of the tower and the port from the deck. Around dusk, switch on night mode if the tower is lit, and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The observation deck and cafe are only open during working hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Gwangan Bridge
label: Gwangan Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '누리마루 APEC하우스' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'APEC로' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/382760140: large area 'Gwangan Bridge' (1004 m across): the middle of the area.
notes: Double-deck suspension bridge, lit up at night.

text.description:
Gwangan Bridge, also called the Diamond Bridge, is a double-decked suspension bridge that links Haeundae District with Suyeong District across the bay. The whole structure is 7,420 metres long, with a road surface of about 6,500 metres, which makes it the second longest bridge in South Korea. Building began in 1994 and finished in December 2002. It opened briefly for the 2002 Asian Games and was officially opened in January 2003.

The bridge carries vehicles only, so you photograph it from the shoreline rather than from the span itself. The viewpoint for this shot is the coastal path observation deck around Dongbaekseom, a quieter alternative to the beach views, where the bridge appears alongside Nurimaru APEC House, with Oryukdo island further to the left. The headland, the building and the island give that picture a foreground and some depth.

If you want a head-on view of the whole lit span with the Marine City towers behind, Gwangalli Beach is the classic alternative. Millak Waterside Park gives a closer view where the bridge fills more of the frame. Whichever you choose, check the bridge's lighting schedule before you go, because it changes with the season and the day.
text.geographic_location: The viewpoint around Dongbaekseom, beside Nurimaru APEC House, is a separate spot on the coastal path.
text.directions_text: If you want the Dongbaekseom viewpoint with Nurimaru APEC House in the frame, walk from Dongbaek Station Exit 1 to the coastal path at Dongbaekseom, about 20 minutes on foot, and follow the path to the observation deck by the APEC House. A taxi to the Dongbaekseom area saves the walk if you are short of time. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the bridge and the coast sit in one frame. At the Dongbaekseom viewpoint, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want Nurimaru APEC House and Oryukdo in the shot too. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter picture of the bridge, which is a long way off.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 누리마루 APEC하우스 (coastal path observation deck around Dongbaekseom, Haeundae side). The bridge framed alongside Nurimaru APEC House, with Oryukdo further left.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bridge on a lower third line, leaving the sky and sea above it. If you go to the Dongbaekseom viewpoint, keep Nurimaru APEC House at one edge so it frames the view, and let Oryukdo anchor the left side. If you have time, the Gwangalli Beach and Millak Waterside Park views are good alternatives for a head-on or closer shot of the lit span.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights do not burn out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the phone steady. Pinch-zoom only as far as the telephoto lens goes, because digital zoom beyond that blurs the detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around dusk, when the bridge lights come on and the sky still has some colour. The lighting schedule changes by season and day, so check before you go.

text.access_note: The Dongbaekseom viewpoint is on a free coastal path; check the official site before you go for any visiting rules at Nurimaru APEC House itself.

name: Taejongdae
label: Taejongdae
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Cliffs and lighthouse at the southern tip of Yeongdo.

text.description: Taejongdae is a natural park at the southernmost point of Yeongdo District in Busan, and one of the city's best-known places for a day out. The park is thickly wooded with evergreen trees, so the pictures here are mostly about greenery and open outlooks rather than one single building. Facilities for visitors include an observatory, a lighthouse, an amusement park and a cruise ship terminal, which gives you plenty of different subjects within one visit. The name is linked to King Taejong Muyeol (604–661), the 29th king of Silla, who is said to have enjoyed practising archery here after the Three Kingdoms of Korea were unified. The park is listed as Busan monument number 28, together with Oryukdo Island. For your phone, think in layers: dark green trees in the foreground, a path or railing to lead the eye, and the sea or sky behind. The lighthouse and observatory make useful anchor points, because a recognisable shape stops a wide landscape looking empty. Keep your phone straight so any horizon line looks level, and wipe the lens before you start, as sea air can leave a film on it. Allow time to walk, as the park is large and the best views are rarely beside the entrance.
text.geographic_location: Taejongdae sits at the southern tip of Yeongdo District in Busan, on the coast at the southernmost point of the district.
text.directions_text: No Busan metro or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check local transport options before you travel. The phone icon on the map is about 790 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the trees, paths and general scene. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for open outlooks, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the lighthouse or ships in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 790 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to place the horizon on the upper or lower third. Include a path, railing or tree branch in the foreground to add depth. If you take in the lighthouse or observatory, put it off-centre and leave space around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Try a panorama for wide outlooks, moving slowly and keeping the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the trees than midday. Check the weather first, as haze can flatten distant views.

text.access_note: Taejongdae is a public natural park with some visitor facilities; check the official site before you go for current access arrangements.

name: Songdo Beach
label: Songdo Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '송도 구름산책로' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'fountain' (pois); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/474957001: large area 'Songdo Beach' (629 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Korea's oldest public beach with cable car and skywalk.

text.description:
Songdo Beach is a curving stretch of sand on the coast of Busan. It was created by people in 1913 and was the first public beach in Korea. The name Songdo means 'Island of Pines', after the thick pine forest that once covered the island. In 1964 a cable car was built to pass directly over the beach, linking it with Geobuk (Turtle) Island, and cable cars still cross the bay today.

The beach photographs well because several things line up in one view: the soft curve of the shoreline, the cable cars sliding overhead, and the sea on one side with the buildings of the bay behind. The best way to get all of it is from the Songdo Cloud Walkway (송도 구름산책로), a free public walkway over the water. Its glass-floored stretch looks back along the beach, so you can include the cable cars in the same frame. If you want a different picture, the red Yonggung pedestrian bridge over the rocky coast looks down on the shoreline and open water instead of the sand.

Keep a firm grip on your phone while you lean over the rail or the glass floor. Take a few frames with and without people in them, as the walkway can be busy and a figure on the sand gives the beach some scale. Walkways and boardwalks along this coast can close for repairs after storms, so check current access before you plan your visit around them.
text.geographic_location: Songdo Beach is in Busan, with Geobuk (Turtle) Island across the bay, linked to Songdo by the cable car.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check local transport options for getting to Songdo Beach, then head for the beach end of the Songdo Cloud Walkway, by the Songdo Bay cable car station. Once you are on the walkway, the beach is about 1 minute on foot to the east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the curve of the shoreline. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the walkway, the sea and the cable cars all in one frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a single cable car against the sky or the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 송도 구름산책로 (beach end of the walkway, by the Songdo Bay cable car station). A frame of Songdo Beach's curved shoreline and the cable cars crossing overhead, taken from the glass-floored walkway above the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the curve of the beach along the lower third, leaving the upper part for the cable car lines. Use the rail or the edge of the walkway as a foreground line leading into the view. For a different picture, try the red Yonggung bridge over the rocky coast, which looks down on the shoreline and open water instead of the sand.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sand or the cable car to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo as a cable car passes, so you can pick the best moment afterwards. Take a few shots in a row so you can pick the sharpest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the walkway. The beach also looks good at dusk, when you can switch on night mode and steady your phone against the rail.

text.access_note: The Songdo Cloud Walkway is a free public walkway, but parts of the coastal boardwalks may close after storm damage, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nampo-dong
label: Nampo-dong
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jagalchi Market (자갈치시장)' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jagalchi Market' (node/12896054901): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Busy shopping and street-food district with BIFF Square.

text.description: Nampo-dong is Busan's busy central shopping district, in Jung District, and it is a good place to photograph the city's everyday energy. A long north-to-south pedestrian street is lined with shops, cafés and restaurants, with statues and seasonal displays along the way. Heading south, the streets turn into Kangtong Market and Gukje Market, then Jagalchi Market, where seafood is sold and served as the lanes reach the harbour. Two bridges link the area to Yeongdo District across the water. Down at street level it is crowded and the signs crowd the frame, so the best phone shot is from above. Jagalchi Market is the place to head for, where a viewing platform on the upper floors is described as facing the harbour. From there you should get a calmer, raised view of the port and the bridge, with the Nampo-dong waterfront below you. Confirm the platform is open when you arrive. If it is closed, Busan Tower looks down over Nampo-dong's streets toward the harbour and Yeongdo, and Yeongdo Bridge frames the waterfront with the downtown skyline behind it.
text.geographic_location: Nampo-dong is in Jung District, in the southern centre of Busan, next to the harbour and the markets. Two bridges connect it to Yeongdo District to the south.
text.directions_text: Start at the Nampo-dong point in the shopping streets. Head for Jagalchi Market, and check its location against the map before you set off. If you are coming from elsewhere in Busan, go by subway to Nampo Station or by bus, and note that parking around Nampo-dong is difficult and car access is restricted. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the port, the bridge and the waterfront in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge or boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Jagalchi Market (자갈치시장) (viewing platform on the upper floors of the market building, facing the harbor). A quieter, elevated look over the port and the bridge, with the Nampo-dong waterfront below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper third line, so the harbour and bridge fill most of the frame. Include a little of the waterfront below to show the market district. For a different angle, Yeongdo Bridge shows the old bascule bridge with the downtown cityscape behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or water to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky keeps its colour. If you shoot through glass, hold the lens close to it to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and try late afternoon for softer light over the harbour. Check that the platform is open before you go.

text.access_note: Jagalchi Market is a working market, so check the official site before you go and confirm the upper-floor platform is open.

name: United Nations Memorial Cemetery
label: UN Memorial Cemetery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '유엔기념공원' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '재한국 국제연합 기념공원' (way/476626810): edge nearest the subject (671 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/476626810: large area 'United Nations Memorial Cemetery in Korea' (672 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Memorial to UN soldiers of the Korean War.

text.description:
The United Nations Memorial Cemetery in Busan is the only United Nations cemetery in the world. It holds about 2,300 graves of servicemembers who died in the Korean War, laid out over roughly 14 hectares on a green hillside. The graves are grouped into 22 plots by nationality, and the national flags rise above them. For a phone photographer, the main pull is order. Rows of matching white markers run away from you across the lawn, and flags give the frame height and colour.

The quiet is part of the picture, so keep your phone work discreet. The best frames come from the central paths between the national plots. Look down the rows and let the paths lead the eye towards the flags. The curved Wall of Remembrance, finished in 2006, is a good second picture. It carries 40,896 names on 140 marble panels around a central fountain, with lawns and trees around it.

Photography is generally fine outdoors, but not inside the memorial hall. Stay off the grass, avoid photographing people or ceremonies, and do not fly a drone. A daily flag ceremony takes place here, so treat it as something to watch rather than to film.
text.geographic_location: The cemetery is at Tanggok in Nam District, Busan, on a hillside.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot, so head for the Tanggok area of Nam District. Show the Korean name, 유엔기념공원. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the rows of graves and the flags together. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to squeeze the rows closer and pick out a single flag above the markers. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole wall or plot in one frame, and keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (along the central paths between the national plots, looking down the rows of graves). Rows of white grave markers on the green hillside, with the national flags of the contributing countries rising above the plots. The subject lies a short way to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place a path or a row of markers on a line leading into the frame, with the flags in the upper third. Keep your feet on the path. For a second picture, try the curved Wall of Remembrance around its fountain, framed by lawns and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest white marker to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the stone keeps its detail against the green. Skip portrait mode, Live Photos and panorama here, as people and ceremonies are best left out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is given for this spot. Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually suits the white markers and avoids harsh glare, so check the cemetery's visiting times first.

text.access_note: This is a working memorial ground: outdoor photography is generally allowed but not inside the memorial hall, and commercial or published use may need consent, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nurimaru APEC House
label: Nurimaru APEC House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nurimaru APEC House' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W239280379 (Nurimaru APEC House): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Nurimaru APEC House is a glass-fronted building on the Busan shoreline, with the sea and the coast stretching out behind it. It photographs well because the clean, modern building sits so close to the water, and a traditional Korean garden next to it gives you a softer, greener foreground. This is the phone icon on the map. The garden has a gazebo and a sundeck beside the building, facing the sea, and it is a quieter alternative to the lighthouse angle. A photo-taking area here also faces what one guide calls the best view of Busan.

From the garden side, you can frame the glass front with the sea and coastline behind it. Use the gazebo or the sundeck rail to give the picture a foreground and a sense of depth. If you want the classic wide view of the building with the Gwangan Bridge behind it and the sea at dusk, the alternative is Dongbaekseom Lighthouse, which is another viewpoint on the map. Take a few frames here first, and check the route to the lighthouse separately if you want to go there too.

Glass can reflect the sky and throw bright patches into your photo, so shift a step or two sideways until the reflections look calmer. Keep your phone level using the gridlines, as the building has strong horizontal lines that look odd if tilted. Photography inside the exhibition areas may be restricted by signage, so follow any notices once you are indoors.
text.geographic_location: Nurimaru APEC House stands on the Busan coast, next to the sea. Dongbaekseom Lighthouse is another viewpoint on the map.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so you do not need to walk any further once you are there. Look for the traditional Korean garden and sundeck beside the building, on the sea side. If you want the lighthouse view as well, Dongbaekseom Lighthouse is the other viewpoint on the map, so check the route to it separately. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the glass-fronted building with the sea behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the gazebo or the sundeck and want to fit in the garden, the building and the water together. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the coastline or details on the glass front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Nurimaru APEC House itself, in the traditional Korean garden and sundeck beside the building, facing the sea. From here the photo shows the glass-fronted building with the sea and coastline behind it, framed from the garden side. If you want the wider shot with the Gwangan Bridge, Dongbaekseom Lighthouse is the alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's horizontal edges with them so it looks straight. Use part of the gazebo or the sundeck rail at the edge of the frame as a foreground. Leave the sea and the coastline in the upper part of the picture so the building has room to breathe. If you are not happy with the garden angle, try the lighthouse view of the building with the Gwangan Bridge behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glass front to set the focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the sea looks too bright. If reflections on the glass are distracting, move a step or two sideways and take the photo again.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk is recommended for the lighthouse view with the sea. For the garden side, check on the day.

text.access_note: The building is reported to be free to enter, but opening times may vary and photography inside the exhibition areas may be limited by signage, so check the official site before you go.

name: Busan Harbor Bridge
label: Busan Harbor Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '우암동 도시숲' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '우암 도시숲' (way/475866689): middle (350 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/7241587087: the OpenStreetMap point 'Busan Harbor Bridge'.

text.description: Busan Harbor Bridge (부산항대교) links Yeongdo District and Nam District across the harbour, and it was completed in April 2014. A low hill gives you a gentle, slightly painterly view of the bridge. A moon-shaped photo sculpture stands in the foreground, which works well for a silhouette of a friend or family member with the bridge behind. The climb is short and the road up is gentle, so it suits visitors who don't want a hard hike. Be aware that the names get mixed up: the bridge is also called Busan Port Bridge or 북항대교, and some guides confuse it with the Gwangan and Namhang bridges, so check you are looking at the right one. The bridge is a good way off, so it will look fairly small in a wide shot. Use the sculpture to add scale and let the bridge be the backdrop. Take a few frames with the sculpture large and a few with the bridge as the main subject.
text.geographic_location: In Uam-dong, in Nam District, on the hilltop of the urban forest. The bridge itself spans the harbour between Nam District and Yeongdo District.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for the urban forest (우암동 도시숲) in Uam-dong, Nam District, and check the route on a map app. The road up is gentle and the climb to the top is short. Follow it to the hilltop and the moon-shaped sculpture. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the sculpture, the hill and the bridge together. Then try the telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x if your phone has it) to bring the distant bridge closer and fill more of the frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the sculpture to look big in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 우암동 도시숲 (hilltop of the urban forest, Uam-dong, Nam-gu). The bridge framed from a low hill with a moon-shaped photo sculpture in the foreground, useful for a figure silhouette. Place yourself so the sculpture sits in front of the bridge, which gives a ready-made frame for a figure silhouette.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the sculpture on one third of the frame, with the bridge along the opposite line. Ask a companion to stand inside or beside the moon shape for a silhouette, and crouch slightly so they stand against the sky. For a different angle, 청학배수지전망대 shows the bridge head-on from a lawn and wooden deck, but it is a separate stop.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge or sky to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so a silhouette stays dark and the sky keeps its colour. If you shoot after dark, use night mode and rest your phone on a rail or wall to keep it still. Check lighting and path conditions on the day, and take care.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk is a good choice for a silhouette against a softer sky. Check lighting and path conditions on the day, and plan accordingly if you stay after dark.
